newsitem.title: AUSTRIA: FOCUS - OPEC agrees six-month quota freeze.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - OPEC agrees six-month quota freeze.

text.p: OPEC oil ministers agreed on Thursday to a new six-month freeze of their oil output quotas, a measure they hope will keep petroleum prices high despite Iraq's likely resumption of exports.

Agreement to retain a production ceiling of 25.03 million barrels a day (bpd) until the end of next June was announced at the close of a meeting in Vienna of the Organisation of the Petroleum Exporting Countries (OPEC) by the organisation's secretary-general Rilwanu Lukman of Nigeria.
Oil prices stayed firm on the news with benchmark North Sea Brent Blend crude trading just below $22.90 a barrel.

Crucial to the market was news that output by the biggest exporter, Saudi Arabia, remains capped at 8.0 million barrels a day. The Saudis, with additional capacity of 2.0 million bpd in mothballs, are the linchpin of the world oil market.

OPEC met in Vienna as the U.N. Security Council made fresh progress towards easing its Gulf War ban on Iraqi oil sales. A council committee on Wednesday approved a pricing formula to remove one of the final hurdles to an oil-for-food deal with the Iraqis.
Iraq's chief OPEC delegate, Osama al-Hiti, said he expected to resume oil sales within "a matter of weeks".
"If the tanker comes tomorrow we can fill it up", he said.

Baghdad, which hosted the 1960 meeting that created OPEC, has not been allowed to sell oil since it invaded fellow founder member Kuwait in 1990. The U.N. accord would let it sell $2 billion worth to buy food and medicine.

OPEC is currently enjoying a bonanza of strong oil prices, partly because of delays in implementing the U.N. deal caused by Iraqi President Saddam Hussein sending troops into northern Iraq during Kurdish faction fighting in September.
Oil firms are also scurrying to replenish the West's depleted stocks of winter heating fuel.
An oil price of almost $23 per barrel compares with only $18 when OPEC last met in June, and the oil ministers were not inclined to make any rash moves at their conference.
"As for what prices do next," said Geoff Pyne, an energy economist at UBS Ltd in London, "The OPEC portion of world oil supply is now effectively fixed".
"So it depends on how demand balances with the return of Iraq on which the timing is important".
Iraq's Al-Hiti said only "very minor technicalities" needed to be ironed out before Iraq can export 700,000 to 800,000 barrels a day, using up in full his OPEC quota allocation.
Hanging over the OPEC feast was concern that quota violations have already lifted actual output almost one million bpd above its agreed ceiling of 25.03 million, even before Iraq sells any oil.

Quotas for all except Iraq have not changed since 1993, yet output has crept up to almost 26 million barrels. Venezuela alone is alleged to be busting its mandatory limit by as much as Iraq is likely to sell.
Iran's Gholamreza Aqazadeh aired that matter in a bilateral session on Wednesday with Erwin Arrieta of Venezuela. He said the Venezuelan denied being over quota by a single barrel.
But Saudi Arabia is said by a Gulf source to believe that the market is robust enough to absorb more oil because heating fuel stocks are so low.
"Demand is whatever OPEC produces," this source said.
